eras.name: First compilers
eras.background: Programs were written in machine code, and few believed a compiler could match a skilled programmer. FORTRAN proved one could, and Lisp showed that memory could be reclaimed automatically.

eras.name: Compiler theory
eras.background: Optimizations had grown as a collection of separate techniques. Researchers recast programs as graphs, so one general analysis could serve many optimizations. Milner gave typing a formal theory in which types are inferred rather than declared.

eras.name: Managed runtimes
eras.text: Compiling and collecting at run time
eras.background: Object-oriented, garbage-collected languages were flexible, but they ran slowly. Generational collectors and SSA-based optimizers cut the cost, and Self compiled hot code for the types it saw. Java's HotSpot VM, still the core of OpenJDK, brought these ideas together.

eras.name: Reuse and safety
eras.background: Compilers were monolithic, so every new language rebuilt the same optimizer and code generator. LLVM made those parts reusable, and MLIR later extended them to machine-learning hardware. C and C++ memory bugs caused most security flaws, so Rust and WebAssembly made safety the default.

nodes.label: FORTRAN
nodes.problem: Programs were hand-coded in machine language, and few believed a compiler could match a skilled coder.
nodes.idea: Backus's IBM team compiles math-like formulas and optimizes loops and registers to rival hand-written code.
nodes.impact: Soon produced most code at IBM 704 sites, and programs could move to any machine with a compiler.

nodes.label: Lisp GC
nodes.problem: List programs in languages like IPL had to erase every unused cell explicitly.
nodes.idea: McCarthy's Lisp marks every cell still reachable and returns the rest to free storage automatically.
nodes.impact: Freed programmers from manual erasure, and Smalltalk, Java and JavaScript later made collection standard.

nodes.label: Flow analysis
nodes.idea: Frances Allen at IBM represents a program as a graph and computes facts along its edges.
nodes.impact: Kildall soon unified such analyses into one algorithm, the basis of modern optimizing compilers.

from.why: Its flow analysis existed only to assign index registers within that one compiler.

nodes.label: Type inference
nodes.problem: Untyped Lisp hid type errors until run time, while strict type systems ruled out generic code.
nodes.idea: Milner's algorithm infers polymorphic types for ML at compile time, and well-typed programs cannot go wrong.
nodes.impact: Haskell and Rust base their type inference on it, so many type annotations become optional.

nodes.label: Generational GC
nodes.idea: Most objects die young, so Ungar's Smalltalk collector scavenges a small young area often.
nodes.impact: Pauses became unnoticeable, and generational collectors became the default in Java's HotSpot and V8.

from.why: Each collection traced the whole heap and stopped the program, which ruined interactive use.

nodes.label: SSA
nodes.idea: Give each variable a single assignment, merging values at joins, and build it fast with dominance frontiers.
nodes.impact: SSA became the usual form for optimizers, used in HotSpot, LLVM, GCC and Go.

from.why: Tracking which assignments reach each use took large tables that were costly to update.

nodes.label: Self
nodes.problem: Dynamically typed object-oriented languages ran far slower than C, since compilers could not see types.
nodes.idea: Self's inline caches record the receiver types at each call site, and hot code is recompiled for them.
nodes.impact: Type feedback still drives optimizing compilers such as V8's for JavaScript.

nodes.label: HotSpot
nodes.idea: Sun's Java VM interprets code first, then compiles the hot methods using profiles of observed types.
nodes.impact: Adaptive JIT compilation reached everyday programming, and HotSpot still runs Java inside OpenJDK.

from.why: Supplied adaptive optimization, which compiles only the hot code using types seen at run time.
Supplied the form of the server compiler's intermediate representation.

nodes.label: LLVM
nodes.idea: Lattner and Adve define a typed SSA code representation, with the compiler built as reusable libraries.
nodes.impact: Clang, Rust and many other languages and tools now share its optimizer and code generators.

from.why: SSA optimizers sat inside monolithic compilers whose parts no other tool could reuse.

nodes.label: Gradual typing
nodes.idea: Siek and Taha let typed and untyped code mix, inserting run-time checks where they meet.
nodes.impact: Python's type hints build on its theory, and adding types piece by piece, as TypeScript does, went mainstream.

from.why: Static typing was all or nothing, so dynamic code could not adopt types piece by piece.

nodes.label: Rust
nodes.idea: Mozilla-backed Rust checks ownership and borrowing in its type system, ruling out memory errors without a collector.
nodes.impact: Linux and Android adopted it, and Android's memory-safety bugs fell as new code used safe languages.

from.why: Collectors cost control over memory layout, so browsers and operating systems stayed in C and C++.
Supplied a mature optimizer and code generator, so Rust did not need its own.

nodes.label: WebAssembly
nodes.idea: Browser vendors jointly design a compact bytecode with formal semantics that validates fast and runs safely.
nodes.impact: All major browsers shipped it together, and C, C++ and Rust programs now run on the web.

from.why: Emscripten compiled C and C++ through LLVM into asm.js, a JavaScript subset that fell short as a target.

nodes.label: MLIR
nodes.idea: Google's MLIR lets compilers define dialects at many levels of abstraction and lower between them in one framework.
nodes.impact: Triton, OpenXLA, IREE and the Mojo language build on it, as do chip design tools.

from.why: Its single low-level IR suited C-like code, so ML frameworks and languages built private IRs above it.

main.title: Stanford CS143: Compilers
main.why: Lexing, LL and LR parsing, semantic analysis and type checking, runtime organization, code generation, dataflow optimization, register allocation and garbage collection. In English.

further.title: The FORTRAN Automatic Coding System
further.why: Hand-coding dominated the cost of scientific computing, so FORTRAN compiled math-like programs and used flow analysis to assign registers about as well as people.

main.title: Efficiently Computing Static Single Assignment Form and the Control Dependence Graph
main.why: Optimizers kept tracing which assignment reaches each use, so SSA form gives every variable a single assignment and places merges at dominance frontiers.

main.title: LLVM: A Compilation Framework for Lifelong Program Analysis & Transformation
main.why: Compilers optimized once behind a private IR, so LLVM keeps an SSA representation that tools can optimize again at link time and run time; its typed pointers have since become opaque.

further.title: BOLT: A Practical Binary Optimizer for Data Centers and Beyond

main.title: MLIR: A Compiler Infrastructure for the End of Moore's Law
main.why: Each domain-specific compiler rebuilt its own IR stack, so MLIR lets dialects at different levels of abstraction share one infrastructure and lower into each other.

main.title: Optimizing Dynamically-Typed Object-Oriented Languages With Polymorphic Inline Caches
main.why: Dynamic dispatch hides types from the compiler, so polymorphic inline caches record each call site's receiver types and hot code is recompiled for them.

main.title: Maglev - V8's Fastest Optimizing JIT
main.why: TurboFan arrives too late for code that is only warm, so V8 added Maglev, a quick optimizing tier built from bytecode and type feedback.

main.title: OCaml Programming: Correct + Efficient + Beautiful
main.why: Untyped programs fail at run time and typed ones need annotations, so Hindley-Milner turns a program into type equations and solves them by unification.

further.title: A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming
further.why: Untyped programs fail at run time and typed ones need annotations, so Milner's algorithm W infers polymorphic types, and well-typed programs cannot go wrong.

main.title: Gradual Typing for Functional Languages
main.why: Static and dynamic typing each suit different tasks, so gradual typing lets typed and untyped code mix, checking at run time where they meet.

main.title: Getting to Go: The Journey of Go's Garbage Collector
main.why: Go wanted short pauses without moving objects, so its collector went concurrent and dropped generational designs whose always-on write barrier cost too much.

further.title: Why Discord is switching from Go to Rust

further.why: FollowFeed's huge heap stalled G1 and non-generational ZGC, so LinkedIn flattened cached objects to cut headers and allocations, then moved to generational ZGC.

main.title: Safe Systems Programming in Rust
main.why: Systems code needs control without memory bugs, so Rust checks ownership and borrowing at compile time and confines unsafe code behind safe APIs.

further.title: Eliminating Memory Safety Vulnerabilities at the Source

main.title: Threads Cannot Be Implemented as a Library
main.why: Compilers can break correct threaded code when threads come from a library, so Boehm argues C and C++ must define a memory model.

further.title: Foundations of the C++ Concurrency Memory Model

main.title: Bringing the Web up to Speed with WebAssembly
main.why: JavaScript was a poor compilation target, so the browser vendors designed WebAssembly, a bytecode with formal semantics that validates fast and runs near native speed.

further.title: A new way to bring garbage collected programming languages efficiently to WebAssembly

further.why: Prime Video's JavaScript app ran slowly on many TVs, so Amazon moved its low-level systems to Rust compiled to WebAssembly, beside the JavaScript VM.

main.title: Scaling Static Analyses at Facebook
main.why: To catch crashes and security bugs before code ships, Facebook runs compositional analyzers, Infer and Zoncolan, on every code change and comments during code review.

further.title: Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google

further.why: Go's nil checker found only obvious dereferences, so Uber's NilAway infers nilability across functions as constraints and reports contradictions on every build.
